On the earlier night, Udayaditya is the commanding liberator: he confronts Sitaram, draws his sword, and forces or persuades the loyal guard to yield his weapon and be bound so that he can help Ramchandra escape. On the later night, their roles reverse: imprisoned and helpless, Udayaditya is led—or nearly carried—out by Sitaram, who now knowingly enables his escape. The man whom Udayaditya once overpowered and spared becomes his rescuer, while the prince follows his lead, asking what to do and where to go.

Pratapaditya initially orders two Pathan assassins to kill Basanta Ray on the road as he lodges at Simultali on his way to Jessore, but the plot fails when the appointed killer refuses to murder him. Later, acting on Pratapaditya’s signed death warrant, Muktiyar Khan’s men enter Raigarh in disguise, and Abdul kills the old king with a sword while Basanta Ray is praying.

At Jessore, Rammohan assaults and throws him out while Ramai is disguised as a middle-aged woman in the royal women’s quarters; later at Chandradwip, in the king’s chamber with no disguise, Rammohan grabs him by the scruff of the neck and hurls him out of the room.
Rukmini, posing as Mangala, secretly prepares a poison disguised as medicine and sends it through the Rajmahishi’s servant; Surma takes it and dies before she can be exiled.

Her refusal is taken as an intolerable insult, prompting her husband to marry another woman; when Vibha finally arrives in Chandradwip, she discovers she has no home or place in his palace and all her hopes of marital happiness are destroyed.

Rukmini persuades Udayaditya to give her his signet ring. Sitaram and Bhagavat then use its engraved royal seal to stamp a forged petition purporting to be Udayaditya’s complaint to the Emperor, accusing Pratapaditya of treason and seeking his own accession. Bhagavat delivers the petition to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted it from one of Udayaditya’s servants. The seemingly authentic seal makes the fabrication convincing enough for Pratapaditya—despite his doubts—to order Udayaditya imprisoned under guard.

Udayaditya’s forced opening of the palace to enable Ramchandra’s escape leads to the dismissal of the guards Sitaram and Bhagavat. Feeling responsible for their hardship, Udayaditya first gives them money and, after Pratapaditya forbids it, Surma arranges secret stipends for their families. When Pratapaditya learns of this defiance through Mangala, his anger turns against Surma: he orders her sent to her parental home and threatens to imprison Udayaditya if she refuses, compelling her to accept exile.

The song voices Basanta Ray’s desolation: those he loved and sang for are gone, leaving him alone and unable to find joy. He sings it first while quietly watching the sunset at Raigarh, longing for his family in Jessore, and later, after returning to Jessore, as he takes Vibha’s hand before Surma’s empty room and confronts their family’s now-devastated life.

Rukmini’s attempt to stop Udayaditya’s escape fails, but she survives and exposes the escape to Pratapaditya, naming Basanta Ray as an accomplice. She then leads Pratapaditya’s men to Raigarh and remains there, tracking Udayaditya until she can point out his hiding place. Once Pratapaditya confirms that Udayaditya has escaped with Basanta Ray, he sends Muktiyar Khan with an order to execute the king of Raigarh; after Udayaditya is captured, Muktiyar enters the palace and has Basanta Ray killed while he is at prayer.

Pratapaditya initially treats Ramchandra with cold indifference, denying him the ceremonial welcome he expects, interrupting him, conducting official business instead, and dismissing him to the inner quarters—making Ramchandra feel inferior. Later, in his own court, Ramchandra retaliates by allowing and joining ridicule of Pratapaditya as a parvenu of low status whose kingship supposedly depended on Ramchandra’s ancestors and whose family was merely elevated by Ramchandra’s marriage into it.

Rukmini leaves Raigarh, changes her name to Mangala, and settles outside Jessore. Hoping to dominate Udayaditya and the kingdom, she befriends palace servants and exploits his mother’s hatred of Surma: when asked to prepare a potion meant to win him back from Surma, she instead makes poison. Surma takes it and dies before Udayaditya, despite believing she is dying by her own hand. Afterward, Mangala secretly enters his chamber during a storm, exploits his guilt with false claims that he ruined her, and demands his love—later taking his ring as she leaves, after he rejects her advances.

Udayaditya’s lament begins as a rejection of his royal birth: he feels burdened by being Pratapaditya’s heir, judged incapable of ruling, and deprived of fatherly affection and ordinary happiness. His later guilt over the ruin suffered by others because of him deepens this sense of weakness into a desire to leave worldly life altogether. When Pratapaditya declares him unworthy of the kingdom, Udayaditya accepts that judgment and asks to be released from the throne. He then solemnly swears before Ma-Kali never to accept any part of Jessore, sit on its throne, or touch its scepter, naming Samaraditya as heir and renouncing both kingdom and family to become an ascetic in Kashi.

Ramchandra Ray sends Rammohan to deliver a letter renouncing Vibha and forbidding her return to Chandradwip, but Rammohan refuses. The old Nayanchand carries it instead, fears what Pratapaditya may do, and gives it to the Mahishi. She conceals its true contents and shows it only to Basanta Ray, who assumes Ramchandra wrote in anger and that sending Vibha back would soften him.

Basanta advises the Mahishi to announce that Ramchandra has requested Vibha’s return. She does so, reversing the letter’s meaning. Vibha, believing her husband has forgiven her and lovingly summoned her, is overjoyed, trusts in his love, and becomes impatient to go to Chandradwip, unaware that he actually repudiated her.

Pratapaditya locks the palace gates and blocks the adjoining canal with large sal-wood logs, aiming to trap Ramchandra in the palace or stop his boat. But Udayaditya forces open the guarded passage, and Rammohan lowers Ramchandra from the palace roof by an improvised rope directly into the sixty-four-oared boat. The boatmen then haul the boat over the logs and escape while the guards’ weapons and delayed pursuit prove ineffective.

Basanta Ray’s sitar embodies the joy and affection that Udayaditya’s suffering steadily deprives him of. On leaving, he plays it furiously to mask his grief, but his tears choke the music, and he leaves the instrument behind, declaring he will never play it again. Later, without Udayaditya and his loved ones, his singing has lost its joy, and he claims the sitar’s broken strings can no longer be tuned—an image of his own spirit becoming irreparable. When he learns that Udayaditya is imprisoned, this earlier withdrawal from music deepens into utter despair: he can barely comprehend the news, repeatedly asks about his grandson’s confinement, and cries out for him to come.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for boldly opposing oppression and intervening for his subjects without considering the consequences. After Surma’s death, grief and a mysterious fear of Pratapaditya stripped away that courage: he hesitated over every action, abandoned attempts to prevent attacks, fled from witnessing a subject’s abuse, and could no longer even give needy people aid openly or secretly.

Sitaram reverses Udayaditya’s wrongful imprisonment—caused by the forged petition he helped Bhagavat create—by exploiting a deliberately started fire to enter the prison, pull Udayaditya out, and lead him away to safety and freedom.

He rescues Ramchandra Ray by carrying him on his back down a makeshift rope from the palace roof to a boat seventy cubits below, gripping the rope with his teeth to free his hands and lower him aboard. Later, after the king insults and disowns the fainted Vibha, Rammohan lifts her bodily from the chamber, carries her outside, and places her unconscious in a palanquin to take her away.

At Jessore, Vibha is elaborately adorned under the Mahishi’s insistence, weighed down with thick gold bangles, a diamond bracelet, a large nose ring, and a carefully arranged coiffure. Though flustered by this splendor, she appears shy, radiant, and brimming with barely restrained joy as she awaits her husband. In Chandradwip, she deliberately discards that queenly display: dressed as an ordinary woman, she refuses a palanquin and approaches the palace like a subject or beggar. Her fallen veil, unnoticed entry, and appearance resembling a maidservant mirror her changed state—no longer a proudly welcomed wife, but a shamed, desperate woman seeking a husband who does not even acknowledge her.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window embodies loss, longing, and the hope of her return: he leaves her place beside it empty and imagines seeing her there. In prison, the window changes into a symbol of freedom, hope, and transcendence; looking through it at the sky and flying birds lets him feel spiritually free despite confinement, while the bed in the dark room becomes his true prison.

Sitaram first approaches Rukmini as a penniless, boastful suitor, winning a loan by trading flirtatious praise and pet names for access to her beauty and money. He forgets repayment, while their playful intimacy turns into secret scheming. When that scheme helps land Udayaditya in prison, Sitaram becomes furious, curses Rukmini, threatens to burn down her house and disgrace her, and sets out to arrange the prince’s escape. Rukmini, humiliated and possessive of Udayaditya, turns the same hatred toward him.

After staging the prison fire and believing Rukmini dead, Sitaram enters her cottage to steal her money. Instead he finds her alive, soaked and shivering, apparently returned from the brink of death. His mockingly affectionate attempt to reconcile enrages her further: she vows to burn him and Udayaditya and consecrate herself with their ashes, fetches a curved blade, and strikes the floor where he had stood. Sitaram barely escapes, then flees because she knows of the rescue and could expose him. Rukmini retaliates by denouncing him to the king and revealing his role in Udayaditya’s escape, completing the transformation from seductive mutual advantage to murderous rage and mutual danger.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a diversion: the guards abandon their posts to save their possessions and fight the flames, allowing him to remove Udayaditya by falsely claiming that the prison is burning. After Udayaditya is safely away by boat, Sitaram turns the diversion into an elaborate cover-up. His accomplices prolong the guardhouse blaze through deliberate sabotage, then ignite the now-empty prison and place bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword inside. Staged reports of Udayaditya’s screams and the collapsing roof, together with the inaccessible, burned-out cell, manufacture evidence of his death. This delays pursuit, makes the authorities blame the guards’ carelessness, and gives Sitaram time to conceal compromising letters and flee with his family—though Rukmini eventually exposes that Udayaditya escaped alive.

Ramchandra Ray dismisses Udayaditya’s rescue of him as only natural and as motivated chiefly by concern for his own sister, Vibha. Rather than feeling gratitude, he joins his courtiers in mocking Udayaditya and Pratapaditya, letting Udayaditya’s self-sacrifice become a target of ridicule in court.

Pratapaditya scoffs at the minister’s warning that angering the Emperor of Delhi could bring an army, treating both the complaint and imperial displeasure as empty threats. Sitaram and Bhagavat then turn that threat into a trap: they forge a petition, stamped with Prince Udayaditya’s seal, accusing Pratapaditya of treason and seeking his kingdom from the Emperor. Bhagavat pretends to have intercepted it on its way to Delhi and gives it directly to Pratapaditya, supplying the supposed proof that his own son had conspired against him—and thus the pretext for imprisoning him.

Vibha’s hair becomes a quiet register of Surma’s care: when the Mahishi forces an elaborate hairstyle on her, Vibha slips away to have Surma arrange it as she likes, showing Surma as an intimate, comforting presence in the palace. The later contrast makes her loss painfully visible. After Surma is gone, Vibha still waits at braiding time for her to come, but evening turns to night and her hair remains unbraided. Eventually Rammohan notices it is unkempt—a sign of both Vibha’s neglect and abandonment of ordinary hope. Thus the hair moves from a bond of affectionate attention to an unadorned emblem of Surma’s irrecoverable absence and the palace’s diminished care.
